runs.prompt: Does the EU AI Act ban facial recognition in public places? Explain the actual rule and cite two real sources. Prefer an official EU source.
runs.answer:
No — not a blanket ban. The EU AI Act prohibits **real-time remote biometric identification** (e.g., live facial recognition) in publicly accessible spaces **for law enforcement purposes**, subject to narrow exceptions and strict procedural safeguards. Other facial-recognition uses may be regulated as high-risk rather than prohibited.

**The actual rule (Article 5(1)(h))**
- The prohibition covers AI systems used for real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement.[1]
- It applies from 2 February 2025, when the Article 5 prohibited-practices rules took effect (six months after the AI Act entered into force).[2]

**Exceptions and conditions**
- Limited exceptions exist under Article 5(1)(h)(i)–(iii), such as targeted searches for victims of trafficking or missing children, prevention of a specific terrorist threat, or identification of suspects of certain serious crimes.[1]
- These uses are not automatic: Article 5(2) requires prior authorization, fundamental-rights impact assessments, notification, and other safeguards.[2]

**Related prohibitions**
- Article 5 also bans scraping the internet or CCTV material to build or expand facial-recognition databases, as well as emotion recognition in workplaces/education and certain biometric categorization practices.[1]

So the rule is a targeted ban on live, law-enforcement facial recognition in public spaces — not on all facial recognition everywhere.

Sources:
[1] AI Act Service Desk, European Commission: “What systems are prohibited under Article 5 of the AI Act?” https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/what-systems-are-prohibited-under-article-5-ai-act-eg-social-scoring-emotion-recognition  
[2] Publications Office of the EU: Guidance Study on Article 5(1)(h) of the AI Act https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/24b979fc-4829-11f1-8095-01aa75ed71a1/language-en

runs.prompt: What changed in the latest iPhone compared with the previous model? Give three changes that matter and cite one hands-on review.
runs.answer:
Compared with the iPhone 17 Pro lineup, the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max changes in three meaningful ways, per The Verge’s hands-on:

- **Variable-aperture main camera:** The main lens now has a variable aperture, with new “pro” controls for more shooting options. [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/tech/986400/apple-iphone-18-pro-max-hands-on-impressions-september-2026-event)
- **More uniform design:** The glass back is color-matched to the aluminum frame, replacing the two-tone look of the iPhone 17 Pro. [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/tech/986400/apple-iphone-18-pro-max-hands-on-impressions-september-2026-event)
- **New colors:** Four finishes—black, silver, glacier (blue), and burgundy. [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/tech/986400/apple-iphone-18-pro-max-hands-on-impressions-september-2026-event)

Screen sizes and the overall aluminum design are otherwise largely unchanged.

runs.prompt: Does the EU AI Act ban facial recognition in public places? Explain the actual rule and cite two real sources. Prefer an official EU source.
runs.answer:
No — not a blanket ban. The EU AI Act prohibits only **real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes**, and even that is subject to narrow exceptions and procedural safeguards. Other facial-recognition uses may instead be regulated as “high-risk” rather than banned.

**The actual rule**
- Under **Article 5(1)(h)** of the AI Act, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is a prohibited practice [1][2].
- There are limited exceptions listed in Article 5(1)(h)(i)–(iii) — for example, to find victims of certain crimes, prevent a specific and imminent terrorist threat, or identify suspects of specified serious crimes — and these require prior authorization and the procedural requirements in **Article 5(2)** [1][2].
- The prohibitions in Article 5 apply within six months of the AI Act’s entry into force [1].
- Broader biometric identification uses not covered by the ban are classified as high-risk under Annex III rather than prohibited outright [3].

**Sources**
- EU Publications Office, *Guidance Study on Article 5(1)(h) … of the AI Act* — covers the prohibition, its exceptions, and Article 5(2) procedural requirements [op.europa.eu](https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/24b979fc-4829-11f1-8095-01aa75ed71a1/language-en)
- European Commission AI Act Service Desk, FAQ on prohibited systems — lists real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement in publicly accessible spaces as prohibited, with limited exceptions [ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/what-systems-are-prohibited-under-article-5-ai-act-eg-social-scoring-emotion-recognition)
